notes:
**Windows** — run `ruze_0.0.27_x64-setup.exe`.
**Linux** — `flatpak install ruze-0.0.27.flatpak`, then `flatpak run com.ruze.chat`.
**Android** — sideload `ruze-0.0.27.apk`. arm64 devices, Android 8.0 or newer.

---

### Added

- **Push to talk on a mouse button, on Linux.** It was Windows only, and the
  reason given was that watching every input event on a desktop is what a
  sandbox exists to prevent. That is true of the sandbox and not of X11: a
  client may ask the X server for *raw* input events, and the server then
  reports every button on every pointer whatever has the focus, before
  deciding where the press is going and then sending it there anyway. So the
  thumb button opens the microphone and still goes back in the browser, the
  same arrangement Windows has, and it needs no permission the app did not
  already have — the Flatpak already holds the X11 socket for the window it
  draws.

  Choosing the button goes through the same watcher. WebKitGTK keeps the two
  thumb buttons for going back and forward in a page and never hands them to
  what is on it, so the picker could hear a middle click and nothing else — it
  now asks the watcher which button was pressed, which is also how you find
  out at the moment of binding one that the watching works.

  Where it goes quiet is a window belonging to Wayland itself. The compositor
  owns input there and hands an X client nothing, so the button is heard while
  an X11 or XWayland window has the keyboard and not otherwise. Nearly every
  game is the first kind. The settings panel says so rather than leaving it to
  be discovered mid-game.

### Changed

- **A call ends when you go away from it.** Half an hour without touching Ruze
  already sets your status to Away; it now also disconnects you from whatever
  voice channel you are in. An open microphone that outlasts the person who
  opened it is a room listening to a room, and neither end can tell — the
  people still in the channel see somebody who left the house an hour ago, and
  the person who left has no idea what it is picking up. Rejoining is the same
  one click it always was, and it is a click somebody present makes on purpose.

  Talking counts as being there. The idle timer watches the window, and a
  person mid-sentence has their hands nowhere near it, so this device's own
  speaking resets the timer the same way a keystroke does — a conversation is
  never hung up on the people having it. Being muted, or only listening, is
  not activity; that is the case this is for.

- **Channels are sealed now unless you ask for an open one.** It was the other
  way round, and the wrong way round: an open channel's messages are plain
  entries in a document every member holds and goes on holding — a write
  capability cannot be recalled — so an open channel is one nobody can really
  be removed from. They keep the document and go on reading it. Sealing is the
  only thing that ends participation rather than announcing it, so it is what
  a new text channel is, and "Open channel" is a box you tick for a room meant
  to be readable by whoever turns up.

  Being let into a server now hands over every key a channel has had rather
  than only the one in use, so joining still means being able to read what was
  said before you arrived. It does not weaken a removal: what a removal rests
  on is that the person removed never receives the key minted *after* it.

  A sealed channel can say otherwise. **Let new members read what came
  before** is on by default and turning it off hands somebody let in later the
  key in use and nothing else, so they see the channel from the day they
  arrive and its past stays with the people who were in it. It is the one
  thing sealing can do that an open channel never could, and it is offered
  only where it means something — an open channel has no keys to withhold.
  Somebody removed is shut out of everything said afterwards either way.

  Voice is untouched — what it carries never goes through the document, so
  there is nothing there to seal. Channels that already exist are untouched
  too: this is the default for new ones, and there is not yet a way to seal an
  open channel after the fact.

- **Whoever runs a server now hands out the channel keys that went missing.**
  Issuing them is best-effort at the moment somebody is let in, because a
  failure there would leave them admitted to nothing — and the note promising
  that opening the server again would repair it described something that did
  not exist. It does now, which matters much more when every channel is
  sealed: one failed handout would otherwise have shut somebody out of a whole
  server for good.

- **The keyboard shortcuts button is only on the window that has those
  shortcuts.** Nearly every key in that list belongs to a channel — send,
  search, reply — and the button sat in the title bar of the friends window and
  of a popped-out conversation as well, where most of the list is a description
  of things that window cannot do.

### Fixed

- **The checkboxes in "Create a channel" were not checkboxes.** A bare `input`
  rule meant for the name field was catching them too, so each one was a
  full-width, padded, bordered box with a tick somewhere inside it, stretched
  to the height of the words beside it. It had been that way for as long as
  the dialog has had a checkbox in it, and the second one made it impossible
  to miss. The rule now applies to the field it was written for, and the
  dialog fits its window again.

- **Removing somebody from a server now actually stops them being heard.** It
  did not, and the reason is a one-word mismatch: a removal is recorded
  against the person — their account, which is every device they own — and a
  message is written by a *device*. Every place that filtered removed members
  looked the author's device up in a list of accounts, never matched, and went
  on showing their messages to everybody. The removal hid them from the member
  list, rotated the keys to every private channel, and changed nothing about
  what they could say in a public one.

  A removal is now expanded to the devices that account speaks through, and
  that is what the channel, the search and the live sync all read by. A
  removal that names a device outright — the only kind servers made before
  accounts have — still applies exactly as it did, and a machine that has
  since been paired to somebody else is not covered, because it is somebody
  else.

  Two things this does not change, both of them properties of a document
  everybody holds rather than bugs: a removed member keeps the history they
  already had, and they go on receiving whatever is written in *public*
  channels afterwards. Private channels are the ones that go dark, which is
  what the key rotation is for.

- **A private channel's files are sealed like its words.** They were not. A
  typed message went into the document encrypted and an attachment went in
  beside it in the clear — carrying the filename, the size, the caption and
  the blob hash, and the hash *is* the file, fetchable from any member holding
  it. So a private channel went dark on removal for half of what was said in
  it and stayed legible for the half with the most in it.

- **Writing to a private channel without its key now fails instead of writing
  in the clear.** If the key had not arrived, or had never been issued, the
  message was written as plaintext — into the one kind of channel where a
  plaintext entry is readable by exactly the people the key rotation shut out.

- **A removed member's own copy now knows.** Nothing told it. The server
  stayed in the rail, the composer went on accepting messages, and the app
  drew them as sent — while every other copy had stopped reading them at the
  moment of the removal. The server is now marked, the channel says so above
  the history, every way of writing to it is refused, and the device stops
  syncing that server the moment the removal arrives.

- **The windows can be resized again on Linux.** Ruze draws its own title bar
  rather than wearing the desktop's, and turning the desktop's frame off took
  the resize border with it — on Windows the window manager keeps an invisible
  one, so nobody noticed, and on Linux there was nothing left to pull on. Every
  window that can be resized now has its own: a strip along each edge and a
  square at each corner that hand the drag straight to the window manager, so
  it snaps, honours the minimum size and shows the cursor the desktop shows for
  its own windows.

- **Escape closes what is open, from wherever the focus is.** It was a promise
  the shortcut list already made and only sometimes kept: every dialog listened
  for the key on its own backdrop, which meant it only heard it while the focus
  happened to be inside — and several of them stop keys escaping the box, so in
  those the key did nothing at all, ever. There is one listener now and the
  dialogs form a stack, so the frontmost thing is what closes: the confirmation
  over the settings goes first and the settings stay, a menu opened over a
  dialog goes before the dialog does, and an Escape aimed at a dialog can no
  longer reach past it and drop the reply somebody was writing.

- **"Leave it where I put it" now means it.** The friends window offers to sit
  in a corner or to stay where you dragged it, but only the corner was ever
  remembered: closing the window with the X destroys it, and a window built
  again from nothing opens wherever the desktop feels like putting it. The
  place is remembered too now, and asked for on the way back in from the tray.
  A place on a monitor that is no longer plugged in is ignored, since a window
  restored onto a screen that is not there is a window you cannot reach.

  Its size comes back with it, whether or not it is pinned — a corner says
  where a window's edge goes, not how much of the screen it takes, and
  widening the list to fit your friends' names is a thing you should only have
  to say once.

  It also no longer appears in the middle of the screen and then jumps into
  place. Only the window itself knows where it belongs, so the move has always
  happened after the window existed; it is now built invisible and shown once
  it has put itself where it goes.
